1.t: Axonotmesis spares the connective-tissue sheath → Wallerian degeneration then regrowth
Three injury grades by severity (neuropraxia / axonotmesis / neurotmesis)
Carpal tunnel spares thenar sensation (palmar cutaneous branch leaves before the retinaculum); pronator teres does not
Thenar pad is the median-localization key: spared = wrist, numb = proximal
Flick sign is the most specific finding for carpal tunnel
AIN syndrome is pure motor → cannot make an “O” sign, no sensory loss
Median = most common UE entrapment
Common peroneal at the fibular head = most common LE mononeuropathy
Deep peroneal = dorsiflexion + first web space; superficial = eversion + dorsum
Common peroneal lesion causes foot drop
Foot drop at initial evaluation = poor prognosis (motor already involved)
A sciatic lesion can also cause foot drop — localize by associated signs
Piriformis vs hamstring discriminators (immediate-on-sitting + resisted knee flexion at 90° + ischial tenderness = hamstring)
Meralgia paresthetica = LFCN under the inguinal ligament; sensory only, normal EMG
NCS/EMG is the most effective test to confirm and grade; treat empirically in a hypersensitive patient

1.1.t: Rib 10 articulates with T10 only — one vertebra
Rib 8 is false by attachment but typical by shape — two independent axes

1.2.t: Sympathetic chain ganglia lie anterior to the rib heads in shared fascia
Restricted rib motion raises sympathetic tone; rib-raising frees the fascia (rationale)
Rib motion drives venous and lymphatic return against gravity (third rib-cage function)

1.3.t: Diaphragm generates ~60% of inspiratory pressure change (primary muscle)
Accessory muscles fire only in forced breathing; forced in = neck/shoulders, forced out = abdominal core
Anterior + middle scalenes attach to rib 1; posterior scalene to rib 2 (reused in Ribs II ME map)

1.4.t: Pump-handle ribs 2–5 increase AP diameter; bucket-handle ribs 6–10 increase transverse diameter
Caliper motion (ribs 11–12) exists because they lack a costotransverse joint → both diameters slightly

1.5.t: A rib SD is named for the position of ease — find the restricted rib, name where it likes to go
Palpate pump-handle ribs anteriorly (sternochondral junction); bucket-handle ribs at the mid-axillary line
Pump-handle pain = sharp/pinprick at costosternal/costotransverse region; bucket-handle pain = deeper aching at the mid-axillary line

1.t: Diaphragm contracts/descends inferiorly on inhalation, relaxes on exhalation
Pump-handle pain = sharp/pinprick at costosternal/costotransverse junctions
Bucket-handle pain = deep, aching, regional at the mid-axillary line
Pump rotates on transverse axis (AP diameter); bucket on AP axis (transverse diameter)
Pain on inhalation = exhaled rib (refuses inhalation); pain on exhalation = inhaled rib
Inhaled rib: space above narrows, space below widens; anterior inferior edge prominent in front
Rib 1 is ~50/50 pump and bucket — assess for both
Caliper ribs 11–12 couple to diaphragm: inhaled rib swings posteriorly and inferiorly
Static prominence infers side of dominance but requires dynamic motion testing

2.t: Naming order: side → rib number → where it lives (inhaled/exhaled) → predominant motion
Name a rib SD for the position of ease, never the restricted direction
Slot 3 (inhaled/exhaled) is the somatic dysfunction itself
B.I.T.E. = Bottom for Inhaled, Top for Exhaled (group-treatment order)
Wrong-end treatment of a group = mechanical brick wall
Rib-dance ME muscles: rib 1 ant/mid scalene, rib 2 post scalene
Rib-dance ME muscles: ribs 3–5 pec minor, 6–10 serratus anterior, 11–12 lat dorsi + QL
Predominance by palpation site: parasternal → pump, mid-axillary → bucket

3.t: Costochondritis = tender junction, no swelling
Tietze syndrome = tender junction PLUS visible edema (swelling is the splitter)
Cervical rib compresses the lower trunk of the brachial plexus → thoracic outlet syndrome
Scapular repositioning test confirms scapular dyskinesis (treat stabilizers, not cuff)
Rib fracture: distal cage compression localizes pain to the fracture site, not under the hand
Shingles = deep burning dermatomal pain, one side, from DRG varicella reactivation
Musculoskeletal is the most common cause of chest pain

4.t: Scapular dyskinesis rehab = PT to strengthen and stretch the scapular stabilizer muscles

1.t: CRPS Type I = no confirmed nerve lesion (was RSD); Type II = confirmed peripheral nerve lesion (was causalgia) — the single most-marked fact
Recognition triad: disproportionate, non-dermatomal, distal pain
CRPS (regional, objective findings) vs fibromyalgia (widespread four-quadrant, no objective findings)
Allodynia (non-painful stimulus) vs hyperalgesia (exaggerated pain from a painful stimulus)
Type I vs II decided ONLY by a confirmed nerve lesion — not severity, not stage

2.t: Fracture = most common precipitant (~42%), classically distal radius/Colles’
Surgery ~12%, nerve entrapment ~7%, spontaneous ~5%
Epidemiologic skew: female 3–4:1; adults UE-predominant, kids LE
Annual incidence 5–26 per 100,000 per year

3.t: Stage 3 = irreversible dystrophy/atrophy; burning pain is in ALL stages (the stage-3 tell is irreversibility)
Central sensitization = NMDA-driven wind-up + receptive-field expansion + loss of GABA/glycine inhibition
Ectopic activity = spontaneous Na-channel firing; ephaptic transmission = synapse-free electrical crosstalk to healthy fibers
Livedo reticularis = lace-like purplish mottling of stage 3 (vasospasm → venous pooling)
Reduced ROM = most common motor finding
Pain perceived centrally in the somatosensory cortex (“the pain is in your head”)
Four symptom domains: sensory, vasomotor, sudomotor, motor/trophic

4.t: A negative sympathetic block does NOT rule out CRPS (positive confirmatory, negative not exclusionary — Spurling logic)
OMT: HVLA with caution (osteoporosis); indirect techniques better tolerated
Bone scan preferred over plain radiographs in stage 1
CRPS is a clinical Budapest diagnosis — no confirmatory test; do not delay treatment for imaging
Multi-agent pharmacotherapy + PT/OT + psychotherapy (throw the book)
Ketamine (NMDA antagonist) for refractory CRPS
Plain radiographs assess bone, not the autonomic nervous system

1.t: C1 has no spinous process and no body (dens “stolen” by C2)
C2 carries the dens; first large palpable SP off the occiput
Vertigo associated with C2 dysfunction (dural attachments)
Diaphragm function via C3–C5 (“C3, 4, 5 keep the diaphragm alive”)
Intrinsic = deep/near axis/precise; extrinsic = far/larger/power

2.t: SCM: ipsilateral sidebend + contralateral rotation
SCM shares CN XI (spinal accessory) with trapezius
Scalenes: unilateral ipsilateral sidebend, bilateral flexion, accessory respiration (ant/mid → 1st rib, post → 2nd rib)
Semispinalis pain presents as pain turning the OPPOSITE way
Bilateral = flex/extend, unilateral = sidebend/rotate template

3.t: Tight most-midline suboccipital (RCP minor) on OAD compression = cervicogenic headache via the myodural bridge
Myodural bridge from RCP minor to intracranial dura (Spine Journal, 1997)
Palpate/translate the articular pillars, NOT the transverse processes (tender, nerves exit)

4.t: The cervical spine does NOT follow Fryette’s Principles 1 & 2
OA = Opposite Always — sidebending & rotation opposite regardless of AP curve; primary motion flexion/extension
AA = ~50% of cervical rotation; full flexion isolates it; diagnosis records rotation only
C2–C7 same-side coupling; C2–C4 rotate more, C5–C7 sidebend more
Push left → sidebend left; limited translation right = restricted left sidebending = lives in right sidebending
3-part diagnosis: Type (N/F/E) + SR + direction of freedom (worked: C3 NSRRR; OA ESRRL)
Cervical superior facets BUM (Backward, Upward, Medial) vs thoracic BUL

1.t: Most common disc herniation = C6–C7 → C7 nerve root (single most common cervical radiculopathy)
Compressive (disc, spondylosis, stenosis) vs non-degenerative (tumor, infection, systemic) etiology buckets

2.t: C5–T1 nerve-root chart (motor/reflex/sensation per root) — highest-yield figure to memorize
C5: deltoid/biceps, biceps reflex, lateral arm
C6: wrist extensors, brachioradialis reflex, thumb/index
C7: finger extensors, triceps reflex, middle finger
C8: finger flexors, no reliable reflex, ulnar 4th–5th digits
T1: hand interossei (finger abduction), no reflex, medial arm
DTR grade 4 = clonus = always abnormal; hyporeflexia = LMN/root, hyperreflexia/clonus = UMN
Pain most intense proximally (neck); paresthesias distal; shooting/electrical, worse with Valsalva
Cervical roots exit ABOVE the like-numbered vertebra through C7; C8 fills the gap below C7

4.t: Spurling worsens (narrows foramen); distraction improves (opens foramen)
Valsalva worsens symptoms with a herniation/mass

1.t: SNS to lungs = bronchodilation, then (over time) vasoconstriction + thickened secretions
PNS/vagus = bronchoconstriction + thinned secretions
Pulmonary sympathetics = T2–T7; parasympathetics = vagus (CN X)
Treat OA / C2–C3 / cranial base to normalize vagal tone (vagus exits skull there)
Chapman point treatment always decreases sympathetic tone to the viscera
Same input, opposite value: SNS good acutely (bronchodilation), bad chronically (vasoconstriction)

3.t: Hering-Breuer reflex = shallow half: airway afferents can't tell air from fluid → fluid-filled lung trips it → limited diaphragm excursion
Carotid body = rapid half: senses hypoxia → drives respiratory rate up
Diaphragm stress → lower six ribs + thoracolumbar junction; T1–T6 paraspinals show increased tone
Phrenic nerve = C3-C4-C5 ('C3-4-5 keeps the diaphragm alive')

4.t: FIRST lymphatic step is always open the thoracic inlet ('easy one on your level one')
No pump techniques until afebrile (pumping while febrile drives cytokines/bacteria before antibiotics cut the load)
Rib-raising >90 s decreases sympathetics (pneumonia); short burst stimulates them (acute asthma)
MOPSE: OMT + antibiotics beat antibiotics alone on length of stay, IV-antibiotic duration, respiratory failure/ventilator, and mortality
Atelectasis: TLP vs incentive spirometry → similar atelectasis rates, but TLP gives better PFTs + earlier recovery — use both

1.t: Cardiac sympathetics arise from T1-T6 (vs peripheral/renal T10-L2)
Increased sympathetic tone increases rate, contractility, and cardiac output
Right hypersympathetic activity drives SVTs (SA node)
Left hypersympathetic activity drives ectopic foci / VF (AV node/ventricle)
Sustained sympathetic tone causes coronary vasospasm (angina without fixed stenosis)
Renal sympathetic stimulation causes water/salt retention and raises BP

2.t: Cardiac parasympathetics travel via the vagus; increased tone lowers rate and contractility
Right hyperparasympathetic activity produces sinus bradyarrhythmias (SA node)
Left hyperparasympathetic activity produces AV blocks (AV node)
Cervical myofascial release shifts sympathovagal balance toward parasympathetic

3.t: Impaired lymphatic drainage reduces collateral circulation and causes congestion-driven arrhythmias
Lymphatic dysfunction linked to atherosclerosis, HTN, and CHF edema

4.t: ALL cardiac OMT is done AFTER emergent medical treatment and stabilization (adjunct, never substitute)
Anterior MI = sympathicotonia T1-T6 (esp. T2-T3 left)
Inferior wall MI = vagal hyperactivity (C2 / cranial base)
HTN: posterior Chapman adrenal points lower BP and decrease serum aldosterone
HTN: renal contribution reduced via sympathetic inhibition at T10-L2
CHF lymphatic return challenged 3-40x; treat T1-T6 plus lymphatic pump/effleurage
Right pectoralis major trigger point drives SVT (postural arrhythmia contributor)
Post-CPR: treat ribs and sternum with indirect techniques

CU.1.t: Organ→cord-level viscerosomatic chart is the high-yield unit ("KNOW CHART")
Kidneys T10–T11 and uterus/cervix T10–L2 (prior-student-highlighted rows)
Hindgut/pelvic parasympathetics = pelvic splanchnics S2–S4; vagus stops at the splenic flexure
Foregut T5–T9 / midgut T10–T11 / hindgut T12–L2 embryologic bands
Appendix = T12; adrenals = T10; all GU = T10–L2

CU.2.t: Standing flexion: PSIS that moves MORE = dysfunctional side
ASIS compression test: less motion / more resistance marks the dysfunctional side
ME levers: anterior→extensors, posterior→flexors, inflare→adductors, outflare→abductors
Anterior innominate = ASIS inferior + PSIS superior; posterior = reverse
Superior shear = ALL landmarks superior; inflare toward midline / outflare away

CU.3.t: Three transverse axes — S1 respiratory, S2 postural, inferior iliosacral
Base posterior on inhalation, base anterior on exhalation

CU.4.t: Seated flexion test positive OPPOSITE the oblique axis
Forward torsion = negative spring + sphinx more symmetrical; backward = positive spring + more asymmetrical
Bilateral flexion = exhalation (deep sulci, posterior ILAs); bilateral extension = inhalation (shallow sulci, anterior ILAs)
ILAs <1 thumb apart = torsion; >1 thumb apart = unilateral ("E elevates, F falls")
L5 rotates opposite the sacrum; L5 sidebends toward the axis

CU.5.t: Board-elimination rule: option E/F → SB+rotation SAME; option N → SB+rotation OPPOSITE; answer must name segments + N/E/F
Law III: inducing motion in one plane restricts motion in the other two
Type I neutral/opposite/group vs Type II non-neutral/same/single
Name the SD for the direction of ease / freer motion, not the restriction

CU.7.t: Won't improve without treating the KEY LESION (flexed L1/L2)
Most-common misdiagnosis = lumbar radiculopathy; psoas → contralateral knee, radiculopathy → nerve distribution to foot
Late-stage S-curve: L1/L2 Type II toward tight side, L3–L4 Type I opposite, pelvis shifts away, piriformis contralateral
Psoas does NOT attach to L5; rehab is extension-biased with NO sit-ups
